transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start time: 15:00 PST
Scheduled duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood, AE); Daniel Cho (Redwood, SE); Maya Patel (Verdigris MedTech, Head of ML); Carlos Ruiz (Verdigris, CTO); Evan Lee (Verdigris, Data Engineer)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Verdigris is evaluating Redwood for inference for clinical-document summarization and multilingual patient-facing Q&A. Key concerns: long context windows (30k+), Spanish/Portuguese support, tool-calling for retrieval + EMR connector, and data residency/compliance. They are comparing hosted vs dedicated vs private for performance and security. Next steps include pricing, trial Dedicated run, and security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm lena from redwood. daniel's here from our solutions engineering team, real quick can folks say how they're joining and a one-line on what you want to get out of this call?
[00:12] Maya: maya here - thanks, we're trying to pick a serving approach for our clinical summarization and triage flows, main questions are model choice (open models), context length needs and multilingual quality, and whether we need Dedicated or Private for compliance.
[00:25] Daniel: great, totally, and just to set expectations we'll talk tradeoffs - latency vs cost, what models support 32k or 100k contexts, tool-calling support for retrieval and connectors, and security controls.
[00:40] Carlos: quick note, our infra folks prefer not to move PHI into vendor-managed buckets if avoidable - so VPC or on-prem considerations matter.
[00:48] Lena: noted. can you share a bit about volumes - avg doc length, qps, SLAs?
[00:56] Evan: mostly long discharge summaries and patient notes - average document ~6-10k tokens, some concatenated threads push above 25k tokens. Peak QPS is low right now, ~5 to 10 requests per minute, but latency target is <1.5s for short queries and <3s for longer summarization where possible.
[01:20] Maya: also multi-lingual - english + spanish primarily, portuguese occasionally. We need consistent hallucination behavior and good factuality for clinical text.
[01:33] Daniel: makes sense. for open models there are options: m-3/llama-3-like families, mistral variants, mosaic models - each has different context support and perf. Redwood hosts curated open models and also offers quantized variants; on Dedicated we can run larger context configs and higher throughput.
[01:55] Carlos: can you clarify which models support 32k or 100k context? We heard m3 has 64k, others have 32k - some of that is marketing.
[02:05] Daniel: yeah there's noise. practical support depends on model + tokenizer + runtime kernel. for instance, some llama3 forks claim 100k but in practice you need careful KV cache and memory planning. Redwood supports up to 100k in Private/Dedicated for certain model builds; hosted has curated 32k and a few limited 64k options. we'll send a model-context matrix.
[02:30] Evan: and tool-calling - we need function-calling for an EMR retriever, plus safe tool sandboxing so we don't leak PHI when calling external services.
[02:40] Lena: Redwood supports structured function/tool calling and can isolate connectors in Private or Dedicated via VPC peering. For Hosted we provide hardened connectors but customers with stricter requirements often choose Dedicated or Private.
[02:55] Maya: security checklist: SOC 2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS for keys, and data residency. Do you have SOC reports and KMS integrations?
[03:06] Daniel: yes, SOC 2 in our security pack, SAML SSO support, RBAC in Console, audit logs are available and we integrate with major KMS/HSM providers. For Private/on-prem we can support customer-managed KMS. we'll attach our security docs.
[03:22] Carlos: what's the cost delta between hosted and Dedicated for these long-context runs?
[03:28] Lena: depends on usage patterns. hosted is per-token and easier to start, Dedicated is a reserved GPU pool (monthly commit) which becomes cheaper at scale and gives you guaranteed throughput and lower tail latency. Redwood Optimize can give batching/quantization recs to reduce unit cost. we'll share a sketch TCO.
[03:46] Evan: on quantization - do you have 4-bit or 8-bit quant profiles that preserve medical factuality? We can't afford hallucinations from aggressive quant.
[03:56] Daniel: we have curated quant profiles, and we recommend running evals on your samples. some models quantize well; others degrade. we can run a pilot comparing FP16 vs 4-bit for a few prompts.
[04:10] Maya: about multilingual - which open models perform best for spanish medical? Llama variants sometimes falter on idiomatic spanish.
[04:20] Daniel: empirically, some mosaic and mistral-large variants fine-tuned on multilingual corpora do better; also instruction-tuning and domain-adaptation matter. we suggest a short eval on your spanish corpus to pick a model.
[04:33] Carlos: what's the typical rollout for a customer like us?
[04:38] Lena: usually start hosted for initial proof-of-concept, then move to Dedicated for predictable throughput and reduced cost, and Private if data residency/compliance requires it. for you, given PHI concerns, many enter via Dedicated with VPC peering and then consider Private later.
[04:55] Maya: timeline - we aim to pilot in Jan, production by April if things look good.
[05:02] Lena: good. do we want Redwood to run a benchmark comparing 3-4 open models (32k/64k variants) on your sample prompts in a Dedicated trial?
[05:10] Maya: yes that would help. include spanish summaries and tool-calling flows.
[05:15] Daniel: noted. small note on tool-calling: some models have limited deterministic function-calling; we recommend a thin deterministic orchestration layer (Redwood supports structured outputs + function schema). we'll test that in the pilot.
[05:31] Evan: on telemetry and cost visibility, we need per-route token breakdown and per-request latency percentiles.
[05:38] Daniel: Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-model dashboards, tracing hooks and error analysis - you can filter by route and see tail latency.
[05:48] Carlos: any gotchas for running very long contexts? memory spikes, KV cache eviction?
[05:55] Daniel: yes, long contexts increase KV cache pressure and memory; runtime kernel selection and batching matter. on Dedicated/Private we can tune VM shapes and kernel configs. also prefix caching and retrieval augmentation reduce effective context size.
[06:12] Maya: about retrieval-augmented generation - we need to ensure we don't leak unrelated patient info when retrieving. Any redwood features for retrieval safety?
[06:22] Lena: we have retrieval policies, redaction options, and the option to route retrieval into a sandboxed connector in Private or Dedicated. we'll demo retrieval redaction patterns in the follow-up.
[06:35] Carlos: competitors - we piloted with openai and anthropec? (sic) last quarter and saw better latency but higher cost. how do you compare?
[06:45] Daniel: compared to hosted big-llm vendors, Redwood's differentiator is predictable unit economics and ability to run specialized kernels on Dedicated. we'll share benchmarks.
[06:56] Maya: also licensing - if we run Private, can we bring our own model weights or do you supply?
[07:03] Daniel: both. on Private you can bring your own weights or we can deploy pre-built images with curated open weights. licensing depends on the model license - we'll walk through specifics if you have a model in mind.
[07:16] Evan: are there existing connectors for Epic/athena? (possible transcript noise)
[07:22] Lena: we have standard retriever connectors and can build custom connectors; for EHR systems we typically do a secure connector project during integration.
[07:30] Maya: any examples of similar medtech customers?
[07:34] Lena: we have several healthcare customers (non-identifying), and we can share redacted benchmark notes and architecture patterns.
[07:42] Carlos: what about latency targets for 32k contexts - is <3s realistic?
[07:48] Daniel: for generation of medium length summaries, with tuned kernels and dedicated GPUs it's achievable; hosted might have higher tail latency. we'll measure in the pilot.
[07:58] Maya: ok on next steps - can you outline what you'll send after this call?
[08:03] Lena: sure: 1) pricing and TCO sketch, 2) model-context matrix + recommended models for spanish med, 3) security pack (SOC2, SAML docs, KMS integrations), 4) proposed pilot plan + timeline.
[08:15] Maya: perfect. we'll get sample prompts over by Friday.
[08:20] Carlos: timeline alignment - can we tentatively book a security deep-dive with our infra team next week?
[08:26] Lena: yes we'll propose times.
[08:29] Daniel: i'll start provisioning a Dedicated trial cluster and will need an NDA + some infra details; also please flag any specific models you want tested.
[08:38] Maya: we'll share details. thanks.
[08:42] Lena: thanks everyone. recap - send pricing, security docs, model matrix, and Daniel kicks off perf tests.
[08:50] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional name mis-transcriptions (e.g., anthropec -> Anthropic), and some technical terms may be slightly off.
